CSTS: A Canonical Security Telemetry Substrate
for AI-Native Cyber Detection

Abdul Rahman Email: arahman@alum.howard.edu
Abstract

AI-driven cybersecurity systems often fail under cross-environment deployment due to fragmented, event-centric telemetry representations. We introduce the Canonical Security Telemetry Substrate (CSTS), an entity-relational abstraction that enforces identity persistence, typed relationships, and temporal state invariants. Across heterogeneous environments, CSTS improves cross-topology transfer for identity-centric detection and prevents collapse under schema perturbation. For zero-day detection, CSTS isolates semantic orientation instability as a modeling, not schema, phenomenon, clarifying layered portability requirements.

Index Terms: 
Cybersecurity telemetry, Entity-centric modeling, Knowledge graphs, Security data integration, Representation learning, Zero-day threat detection, Anomaly detection, Telemetry normalization, Cross-environment generalization, Enterprise security architecture

I Introduction

Machine learning and graph-based methods are now widely used in cybersecurity for tasks such as lateral movement detection, anomaly discovery, and zero-day threat detection [1, 2, 3, 4]. In controlled settings, these approaches can achieve strong performance; however, operational deployment remains difficult. Models that work well in one enterprise environment frequently degrade when moved to another, even when the underlying threat behaviors are similar. This degradation often persists across changes in topology, telemetry vendors, and logging configurations, suggesting that the limiting factor is not model architecture alone.

A primary source of deployment friction is telemetry representation. Enterprise security data is fragmented across heterogeneous vendor schemas, event-centric formats, and environment-specific pipelines. Normalization frameworks such as the Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework (OCSF) [5] reduce syntactic inconsistency and improve cross-vendor field alignment, but they remain fundamentally event-focused: higher-order constructs required for portable learning systems—persistent entity identity, typed relational semantics, and explicit temporal state—are typically reconstructed downstream on a per-environment basis. As a result, detection systems repeatedly re-implement identity stitching, relationship extraction, and feature logic for each deployment, creating brittle coupling between detection logic and telemetry idiosyncrasies.

We view this as a representational gap: the absence of a canonical abstraction layer between raw telemetry ingestion and downstream analytics. Without such a substrate, portability failures conflate multiple mechanisms. Some failures arise from schema instability (e.g., missing fields, renamed columns, vendor drift). Others arise even when schema is aligned: features derived from relational structure can change their meaning under domain shift, producing semantic orientation instability where class-conditional feature direction reverses across environments. Distinguishing these mechanisms is essential for building robust AI-native security systems.

In this work, we introduce the Canonical Security Telemetry Substrate (CSTS), an entity-first, relationship-explicit representation layer that formalizes (i) persistent canonical identities, (ii) typed interactions as first-class relations, and (iii) temporally indexed state suitable for downstream statistical, graph, and learning-based detectors. CSTS is designed as a stable integration boundary: heterogeneous telemetry sources are mapped into canonical entities and typed relationships via thin adapters, and detection systems consume CSTS primitives rather than vendor-specific event fields.

We empirically evaluate CSTS under controlled and external settings. In a synthetic two-environment benchmark (Env A→\rightarrowEnv B) designed to isolate representational effects, CSTS materially reduces transfer degradation for identity-centric detection (lateral movement) relative to an event-centric baseline and remains operable under targeted schema perturbations that cause the baseline pipeline to fail. For flow-centric zero-day detection, CSTS preserves schema alignment but reveals a distinct portability boundary: directional stability of graph-derived statistics under domain shift remains a separate modeling challenge. Finally, on public real-log corpora we include external robustness/smoke tests and a producer-divergence case study (TC E3) to validate pipeline behavior under realistic telemetry heterogeneity and to surface cross-producer distributional mismatch under leakage-safe thresholding.

This paper makes three contributions:

  1. 1.

    Canonical substrate. We formalize CSTS as a governed entity-relational telemetry layer with explicit identity persistence, typed relationship semantics, and temporal indexing.

  2. 2.

    Portability decomposition. We articulate a portability framework that separates schema stability (representation and ingestion invariants) from semantic orientation stability (feature direction invariance under domain shift).

  3. 3.

    Empirical evidence. We provide controlled transfer and schema-perturbation experiments demonstrating improved portability for identity-centric detection, and we document a producer-divergence artifact illustrating that schema alignment alone does not guarantee cross-producer calibration alignment.

II Background

Modern cybersecurity architectures aggregate telemetry from heterogeneous sources including network infrastructure, identity providers, endpoint agents, cloud control planes, and threat intelligence feeds. Although advances in normalization frameworks and machine learning–based detection have improved large-scale analysis, persistent deployment friction remains. Integration overhead, representational instability, and cross-environment degradation continue to limit reliable AI adoption in production environments.

We review three relevant foundations: (i) event-centric normalization frameworks, (ii) machine learning–based detection systems, and (iii) empirical deployment gaps observed in practice.

II-A Event-Centric Normalization

Enterprise telemetry is fragmented across vendors, schemas, and collection pipelines. To address syntactic inconsistency, normalization frameworks such as the Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework (OCSF) [5], STIX/TAXII, Elastic Common Schema (ECS), and related standards align field names and event structures across products.

These frameworks improve interoperability by standardizing event-level attributes such as timestamps, source/destination identifiers, event categories, and metadata fields. In practice, normalization reduces parsing complexity and enables cross-tool ingestion into SIEM and data lake environments.

However, event-centric normalization primarily solves schema alignment. It does not provide higher-order semantic abstraction. Persistent entity identity, typed relationships among entities, temporal behavioral state, and longitudinal role modeling are typically reconstructed downstream within detection pipelines. Consequently, identity stitching is repeatedly reimplemented for each deployment, graph-construction logic becomes bespoke and tightly coupled to specific detection models, and behavioral-aggregation pipelines vary across environments. This fragmentation increases operational overhead and introduces instability into downstream learning systems.

Thus, while normalization frameworks reduce syntactic heterogeneity, they do not define a canonical entity-relational substrate suitable for stable AI-native modeling across heterogeneous deployments.

II-B Machine Learning–Based Detection

Machine learning methods are widely applied to cybersecurity tasks including anomaly detection, lateral movement identification, zero-day discovery, ransomware detection, and insider threat monitoring. Supervised classifiers, unsupervised anomaly detectors, graph neural networks, autoencoders, and metric learning approaches have demonstrated strong performance in controlled settings.

Graph-based models capture relational structure among users, hosts, processes, and network flows. Autoencoder architectures model baseline behavior and identify deviations indicative of novel attacks. Metric learning frameworks structure latent representations to improve separation of attack classes.

Despite their architectural sophistication, these systems often rely on environment-specific preprocessing, feature engineering, and identity-resolution rules. Relationship semantics and behavioral features are often tightly coupled to telemetry idiosyncrasies. As a result, feature definitions become unstable across deployments, transfer performance degrades under topology or vendor changes, and model portability often requires retraining or manual adaptation. These effects collectively undermine the reliability of AI-based detection systems in heterogeneous enterprise environments. These limitations indicate that improvements in model architecture alone are insufficient without a stable representational boundary between ingestion and detection.

II-C Deployment Gaps

Operational deployment reveals recurring friction beyond model accuracy. Integrating new telemetry sources requires adapter development, identity reconciliation, and reconstruction of higher-order behavioral abstractions. Vendor updates and schema drift introduce ongoing maintenance burden.

Furthermore, graph structures used by detection systems are often rebuilt independently within each pipeline rather than derived from a shared canonical representation. This increases operational complexity and creates tight coupling between ingestion logic and modeling logic.

Cross-environment generalization remains particularly challenging. Models trained in one enterprise topology may degrade when deployed in another due to differences in identity semantics, role distributions, and telemetry coverage—even when schema fields are nominally aligned. This suggests that portability failures may arise from deeper semantic instability rather than schema mismatch alone.

Collectively, these gaps indicate the absence of a canonical telemetry substrate that formalizes persistent identity, typed relationships, and temporal state independent of vendor-specific event formats.

III Problem Statement

Existing AI-driven cybersecurity systems lack a canonical, entity-centric telemetry representation that enables stable deployment and cross-environment generalization. Event-centric normalization aligns fields but does not formalize:

  • •

    Persistent canonical identity across heterogeneous sources,

  • •

    Typed relationship semantics suitable for graph and relational modeling,

  • •

    Temporally indexed behavioral state evolution,

  • •

    Compatibility with embedding- and representation-based learning paradigms.

As a consequence, detection pipelines repeatedly reconstruct behavioral abstractions, graph construction remains ad hoc and model-specific, schema drift and telemetry variation erode portability, and integration overhead slows enterprise adoption. Together, these factors create structural friction that limits scalable and generalizable AI deployment.

We define the central problem as follows:

How can enterprise security telemetry be represented in a canonical, entity-relational form that enables stable deployment, cross-topology generalization, and compatibility with advanced learning paradigms without requiring per-environment reconstruction of behavioral features?

IV Related Work

AI-driven cybersecurity systems operate at the intersection of enterprise telemetry architecture, schema normalization, graph-based reasoning, and learning-based detection. Substantial advances have been made across these domains. However, most prior work implicitly assumes the availability of stable, semantically coherent telemetry representations. We synthesize existing research and identify a persistent representational gap: the absence of a vendor-agnostic, entity-first, relationship-explicit substrate designed explicitly to support portable AI deployment across heterogeneous enterprise environments.

IV-A Telemetry Security Architecture and Enterprise Deployment Context

Enterprise telemetry infrastructures are increasingly recognized as high-value assets requiring layered security controls. Kalibjian emphasizes that telemetry post-processing environments contain sensitive and strategically valuable data, arguing for encryption, key management, and compliance-aligned protections for telemetry at rest and in motion [6].

Zegeye and Odejobi propose a cybersecurity architecture for telemetry networks modeled after ICS/SCADA systems, emphasizing segmentation, zone-based control, and boundary management across enterprise and field layers [7]. Dean et al. further extend this perspective with a networked telemetry security architecture integrating layered controls across distributed enterprise domains, positioning telemetry infrastructure as a foundation for advanced analytics and AI-driven monitoring [8].

These works provide critical operational realism by clarifying how telemetry is generated, transmitted, and secured. However, telemetry is treated primarily as protected data-in-motion rather than as a formally defined representational layer for AI systems. Canonical identity persistence, typed inter-entity semantics, and substrate-level temporal abstraction are not explicitly addressed.

IV-B Telemetry Normalization and Observability Frameworks

Normalization frameworks such as the Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework (OCSF) [5], Elastic Common Schema (ECS) [9], and OpenTelemetry [10] have significantly improved cross-vendor interoperability through standardized event schemas and attribute alignment. These frameworks reduce ingestion friction, simplify SIEM integration, and enable consistent field naming across heterogeneous sources.

Rongali demonstrates how OpenTelemetry instrumentation can be extended with enriched spans and security-oriented attributes to enhance detection fidelity [11]. Such efforts show that structured instrumentation improves contextual signal quality.

However, normalization frameworks remain fundamentally event-centric. They standardize event syntax but do not formalize persistent entity identity across sessions and vendors, canonical inter-entity relationships, or longitudinal behavioral state. Higher-order abstractions required for AI-native detection are therefore reconstructed downstream within environment-specific pipelines. Normalization reduces syntactic variance but does not ensure semantic stability.

IV-C Telemetry Representation and Scalable Security Analytics

Representation-level innovation has sought to elevate telemetry beyond raw event streams. Taylor et al. introduce SysFlow, a compact telemetry format that lifts low-level system events into a flow-centric, object-relational abstraction linking processes, files, and network endpoints [12]. SysFlow improves interpretability and reduces storage overhead by compressing event granularity into relational summaries.

While aligned with the goal of relational abstraction, SysFlow focuses primarily on host-level telemetry and does not generalize across heterogeneous enterprise domains such as identity providers, SaaS platforms, cloud control planes, or threat intelligence systems. Nor does it define governance mechanisms for cross-domain identity persistence or canonical relationship ontologies suitable for stable AI deployment.

Thus, representation compression improves efficiency but does not establish a universal substrate for cross-environment portability.

IV-D Learning-Based Detection and Graph-Oriented Security Systems

Machine learning is central to modern intrusion detection. Okonkwo surveys advanced intrusion detection approaches incorporating behavioral modeling and AI-enhanced anomaly detection in enterprise telemetry networks [13]. Zero-day detection research emphasizes anomaly modeling and behavioral generalization for detecting previously unseen attack patterns [1, 2]. Metric learning approaches structure latent representations to improve discrimination of malicious behavior [2, 14, 15].

Graph-based intrusion detection systems and knowledge graph security models encode entities and interactions to enable contextual reasoning, attack path reconstruction, and campaign analysis [16, 17, 18, 19]. These systems demonstrate that relational structure is essential for detecting multi-stage adversarial activity such as lateral movement.

However, most graph and learning-based systems derive entity graphs and behavioral features from event streams in environment-specific ways. Identity resolution, relationship extraction, and feature engineering remain tightly coupled to vendor schemas and telemetry peculiarities. As a result, portability across enterprises is limited, and deployment frequently requires retraining or re-engineering.

The limiting factor increasingly lies in representational instability rather than model capacity.

IV-E Telemetry Collection and Dataset Generation

Holeman et al. introduce SETC, a containerized framework for repeatable exploit execution and telemetry collection to support controlled dataset generation [20]. SETC advances reproducibility and systematic evaluation of defensive models under known attack scenarios.

However, while dataset generation improves experimental rigor, it does not resolve representational heterogeneity in real enterprise environments. Telemetry collected in controlled settings still requires identity reconciliation and relational abstraction when deployed into heterogeneous operational ecosystems.

IV-F Feature Drift, Domain Adaptation, and Deployment Fragility

Feature and concept drift are well-documented challenges in operational intrusion detection, where evolving traffic patterns and attack behaviors degrade model performance over time [21]. Broader surveys of distribution shift emphasize that deployed machine learning systems require continuous monitoring and adaptation in non-stationary environments [22].

In enterprise cybersecurity, distribution shift is compounded by schema variation, vendor heterogeneity, telemetry incompleteness, and identity inconsistencies across deployments. Existing mitigation strategies focus on retraining, adaptive ensembles, or adversarial robustness, but rarely address representational stability at the telemetry substrate level.

This recurring deployment fragility suggests that the principal bottleneck in AI-driven cybersecurity is architectural rather than purely algorithmic.

IV-G Synthesis: The Representational Gap

Across telemetry security architecture, normalization frameworks, scalable representation formats, graph-based detection systems, and ML deployment research, three themes consistently emerge:

  1. 1.

    Enterprise telemetry is operationally complex and strategically sensitive, requiring secure and governed infrastructure [6, 7, 8].

  2. 2.

    Advanced detection methods rely on stable relational and behavioral abstractions, including persistent entity identity and cross-domain contextual modeling [2, 14, 15].

  3. 3.

    Event-centric normalization frameworks improve ingestion but do not formalize a canonical entity-relational substrate with governed identity persistence and temporal continuity [5, 12, 11].

No surveyed work defines a cross-domain, entity-first, relationship-explicit telemetry layer with persistent identity resolution, typed relational semantics, temporal state continuity, and representational stability contracts designed explicitly for AI portability.

This representational gap motivates the Canonical Security Telemetry Substrate (CSTS), introduced next.

V Design Principles of CSTS

The Canonical Security Telemetry Substrate (CSTS) is designed as an AI-native representation layer that formalizes how heterogeneous enterprise security telemetry is structured before downstream modeling. Unlike event-centric normalization frameworks (e.g., OCSF [5], ECS [9], OpenTelemetry [10]), CSTS is not limited to field alignment. Instead, it establishes stable abstractions for persistent identity, typed relationships, temporal continuity, and governed evolution so that detection models consume a consistent entity-relational state rather than brittle vendor-specific event fields.

CSTS is guided by five design principles.

V-A Principle 1: Persistent Entity Identity

CSTS adopts an entity-first paradigm: security-relevant objects are first-class constructs rather than implicit artifacts reconstructed from events. Canonical entity types include users, hosts, processes, files, network endpoints/flows, credentials, cloud resources, binaries, and externally sourced indicators. Each entity is assigned a persistent canonical identifier intended to remain stable across telemetry sources and time.

This principle targets a central deployment failure mode in event-centric systems: identity instability. In heterogeneous environments, a single logical entity can appear under multiple identifiers across vendors and over time (e.g., hostname aliases, principal-name variants, IP reassignment). When identity is not stabilized, downstream pipelines repeatedly re-stitch entities, producing inconsistent graph construction and degraded cross-environment transfer. CSTS makes identity resolution a substrate responsibility so detection logic can remain vendor-agnostic and topology-portable.

V-B Principle 2: Explicit Relationship Semantics

Security-relevant behavior is fundamentally relational. CSTS therefore materializes typed relationships as explicit substrate constructs rather than deriving them ad hoc inside model pipelines. Relationship types are semantically constrained (e.g., AUTHENTICATES_TO, EXECUTES, SPAWNS, CONNECTS_TO, WRITES, PRIV_ESCALATES) and define permissible source and target entity classes.

By enforcing relationship semantics at the substrate layer, CSTS yields a canonical entity-relational graph that is stable across deployments. Downstream models consume pre-materialized interaction structure rather than rebuilding topology from raw logs, improving reproducibility and reducing environment-specific feature re-engineering. This also enables graph-based learning and reasoning methods to operate over consistent semantics without bespoke reconstruction logic.

V-C Principle 3: Temporal Continuity and Behavioral State

Enterprise security telemetry is inherently temporal: many detection paradigms depend on deviations from historical baselines, sequences of actions, and evolving roles. Event normalization records timestamped events but typically leaves longitudinal state and temporal joins to downstream pipelines.

CSTS incorporates temporal continuity at the substrate boundary by representing entity and relationship state as time-indexed updates. This supports rolling aggregation windows, behavioral baselining, and trajectory-based reasoning in a uniform way across environments. By centralizing temporal semantics, CSTS reduces duplication of temporal aggregation logic across detection systems and improves cross-topology comparability of behavioral features.

V-D Principle 4: Feature Stability and Schema Governance

A recurring cause of enterprise ML fragility is feature instability induced by schema drift, vendor updates, and environment-specific telemetry variance. When features depend directly on raw fields, modest upstream changes can invalidate models or require costly re-integration.

CSTS addresses this through schema governance and feature stability contracts. Canonical behavioral categories (e.g., frequency, diversity, rarity/novelty, privilege spread, role deviation) are defined over canonical entities and relationships and versioned independently of raw event formats. Changes in upstream telemetry are absorbed by adapter-layer mappings and canonicalization policies rather than by modifying model interfaces. This governance approach supports backward compatibility, reduces retraining pressure, and improves operational portability.

V-E Principle 5: Deployment Decoupling and Extensibility

CSTS decouples telemetry integration from detection logic. Vendor feeds are mapped through thin adapters into canonical entities and relationships; downstream consumers then operate on the uniform substrate. This reduces onboarding friction, confines environment-specific work to the mapping layer, and enables incremental adoption.

CSTS is intentionally model-agnostic while remaining ML-compatible: the substrate supports supervised learning, unsupervised anomaly detection, graph learning, metric learning, and embedding-based retrieval. Stabilizing the representational boundary also enables future extensions such as agentic investigation and response workflows over shared canonical state, without requiring structural redesign.

V-F Summary of Design Principles

In combination, these principles shift the representational burden from individual detection pipelines to a shared substrate. Persistent identity, typed relationships, temporal continuity, governed evolution, and deployment decoupling establish CSTS as a foundation for portable, enterprise-ready security analytics across heterogeneous environments.

VI Formal Definition of CSTS

The Canonical Security Telemetry Substrate (CSTS) defines a stable, entity-centric abstraction over heterogeneous enterprise telemetry. Rather than modeling raw vendor events directly, CSTS models security data as a time-indexed attributed multigraph:

Gt=(Vt,Et)G_{t}=(V_{t},E_{t}) (1)

where VtV_{t} denotes the set of canonical entities at time tt and EtE_{t} denotes the set of typed relationships between entities. This abstraction shifts security analytics from event-centric processing to entity–relationship reasoning while enforcing identity, structural, and temporal invariants that promote cross-environment stability.

VI-A Canonical Entities

Let ℰ\mathcal{E} denote the finite set of canonical entity types:

ℰ={\displaystyle\mathcal{E}=\{ Host,User,Process,File,\displaystyle\texttt{Host},\,\texttt{User},\,\texttt{Process},\,\texttt{File}, (2)
NetworkFlow,CloudResource,\displaystyle\texttt{NetworkFlow},\,\texttt{CloudResource},
Credential,ExternalEntity}\displaystyle\texttt{Credential},\,\texttt{ExternalEntity}\}

Each canonical entity e∈Vte\in V_{t} is defined as:

e=(i​d,t​y​p​e,Ae,Se,Te)e=(id,type,A_{e},S_{e},T_{e}) (3)

where:

  • •

    i​did is a globally unique canonical identifier,

  • •

    t​y​p​e∈ℰtype\in\mathcal{E},

  • •

    AeA_{e} is a normalized attribute map,

  • •

    SeS_{e} records source metadata and lineage,

  • •

    Te=[ts​t​a​r​t,te​n​d]T_{e}=[t_{start},t_{end}] is the temporal validity interval.

Entity Invariants

All canonical entities must satisfy:

  1. 1.

    Stable Identity: i​did remains invariant across ingestion boundaries.

  2. 2.

    Schema Normalization: Attributes conform to canonical types.

  3. 3.

    Temporal Explicitness: Validity intervals are explicit.

  4. 4.

    Provenance Preservation: Source mappings and lineage are retained.

Identity Resolution

Let 𝒪\mathcal{O} denote raw telemetry observations. CSTS defines a resolution function:

R:𝒪→i​dR:\mathcal{O}\rightarrow id (4)

such that semantically equivalent observations map to the same canonical identity:

R⁡(oi)=R⁡(oj)⇒oi∼ojR(o_{i})=R(o_{j})\Rightarrow o_{i}\sim o_{j} (5)

Resolution may be deterministic (e.g., normalized identifiers), probabilistic (record linkage), or graph-based (co-reference clustering). All merges preserve lineage and auditability.

Lifecycle Model

Entities transition through time-indexed states:

Created→Active→Dormant→Retired\texttt{Created}\rightarrow\texttt{Active}\rightarrow\texttt{Dormant}\rightarrow\texttt{Retired} (6)

Lifecycle transitions are immutable once recorded and support replay, audit, and historical reasoning.

VI-B Canonical Relationships

Let ℛ\mathcal{R} denote the finite set of canonical relationship types:

ℛ={\displaystyle\mathcal{R}=\{ AUTHENTICATES_TO,EXECUTES,\displaystyle\texttt{AUTHENTICATES\_TO},\,\texttt{EXECUTES}, (7)
CONNECTS_TO,READS,\displaystyle\texttt{CONNECTS\_TO},\,\texttt{READS},
WRITES,MODIFIES,\displaystyle\texttt{WRITES},\,\texttt{MODIFIES},
SPAWNS,OWNS,\displaystyle\texttt{SPAWNS},\,\texttt{OWNS},
ASSOCIATED_WITH}\displaystyle\texttt{ASSOCIATED\_WITH}\}

Each relationship r∈Etr\in E_{t} is defined as:

r=(s​r​c,d​s​t,t​y​p​e,Ar,tr,Pr)r=(src,dst,type,A_{r},t_{r},P_{r}) (8)

where:

  • •

    s​r​c,d​s​t∈Vtsrc,dst\in V_{t},

  • •

    t​y​p​e∈ℛtype\in\mathcal{R},

  • •

    ArA_{r} is a relationship attribute map,

  • •

    trt_{r} is a timestamp or interval,

  • •

    PrP_{r} encodes provenance metadata.

Structural Constraints

CSTS enforces structural constraints to ensure semantic consistency:

  1. 1.

    Type Consistency: Relationship domains and codomains are fixed (e.g., AUTHENTICATES_TO(User, Host)).

  2. 2.

    Directionality: All edges are directed.

  3. 3.

    Temporal Alignment: tr⊆Ts​r​c∩Td​s​tt_{r}\subseteq T_{src}\cap T_{dst}.

  4. 4.

    Cardinality Rules: Optional multiplicity constraints may be enforced.

Provenance Requirements

Each relationship includes:

  • •

    Source system identifier,

  • •

    Ingestion timestamp,

  • •

    Confidence score,

  • •

    Transformation lineage.

This supports auditability, explainability, and forensic traceability.

VI-C Temporal Graph Evolution

Security telemetry is dynamic. CSTS models graph evolution incrementally:

Gt+1=Gt+Δ​Vt+Δ​EtG_{t+1}=G_{t}+\Delta V_{t}+\Delta E_{t} (9)

where Δ​Vt\Delta V_{t} and Δ​Et\Delta E_{t} denote entity and relationship updates, respectively.

Time Semantics

CSTS distinguishes:

  • •

    Event Time (tet_{e}),

  • •

    Ingestion Time (tit_{i}),

  • •

    Valid Time (tvt_{v}).

Attributes may be time-indexed:

Ae​(t),Ar​(t)A_{e}(t),\quad A_{r}(t) (10)

Canonical Aggregation

Aggregation operators are defined over canonical entities and relationships rather than raw vendor events. Supported abstractions include sliding windows, tumbling windows, sessionization, and cross-entity temporal joins. This ensures aggregation semantics remain stable across heterogeneous telemetry sources.

VI-D Learning Objects and Representation Views over CSTS

While CSTS is defined as a time-indexed attributed multigraph over canonical entities and typed relationships, downstream learning systems typically do not consume the full substrate directly. Instead, they operate on bounded relational-temporal units derived from the substrate. To make this interface explicit, we define a learning object in CSTS as a semantically governed, time-bounded view over canonical entities, relationships, and associated state used as the input unit for downstream statistical, graph, or representation-learning models. This extension is consistent with CSTS’s existing role as an entity-first, relationship-explicit substrate designed to support anomaly detection, metric learning, graph-native models, and embedding-compatible AI systems [1, 2, 15].

Formally, let

Gt=(Vt,Et)G_{t}=(V_{t},E_{t})

denote the CSTS graph at time tt, with canonical entities and typed relationships as defined above. A CSTS learning object is a tuple

o=(Vo,Eo,To,Xo,Po,ϕo),o=(V_{o},E_{o},T_{o},X_{o},P_{o},\phi_{o}),

where:

  • •

    Vo⊆VtV_{o}\subseteq V_{t} is a bounded set of canonical entities;

  • •

    Eo⊆EtE_{o}\subseteq E_{t} is a bounded set of typed relationships among those entities;

  • •

    To=[ta,tb]T_{o}=[t_{a},t_{b}] is a bounded temporal support interval;

  • •

    XoX_{o} is the set of canonical attributes and derived behavioral summaries over ToT_{o};

  • •

    PoP_{o} records provenance, adapter lineage, and confidence metadata inherited from the substrate;

  • •

    ϕo\phi_{o} is an optional focalization map specifying the central entity, interaction, or motif around which the object is constructed.

The purpose of this construction is not to introduce a new primitive distinct from canonical entities and relationships, but to provide a stable model-consumption contract over existing CSTS primitives. In other words, CSTS remains ontologically entity-relational, while learning objects provide a bounded computational interface for downstream models.

Several classes of learning objects arise naturally in CSTS.

1) Entity-state objects.

An entity-state object represents the temporally indexed behavioral state of a single canonical entity over a bounded interval. For example, a host-state object may summarize a host’s authentication neighborhood, process activity, file access diversity, and network role over the previous 24 hours. A user-state object may summarize login cadence, peer-host diversity, privilege spread, and role deviation relative to historical baselines. Entity-state objects are especially natural for identity-centric tasks such as lateral movement detection, insider threat modeling, and behavioral risk scoring.

2) Interaction-state objects.

An interaction-state object represents a focal typed interaction together with its source-target context. For example, a focal CONNECTS_TO edge between a process or host and an external destination may be enriched with the source entity’s prior state, the destination neighborhood, recent authentication activity, associated credentials, and bounded graph statistics over an interval ToT_{o}. This object class is particularly useful for flow-centric anomaly detection, zero-day threat detection, and edge-level scoring tasks, especially in settings where graph-aware context improves cross-topology transfer [1].

3) Subgraph-state objects.

A subgraph-state object represents a bounded typed neighborhood around a focal entity or interaction, typically at one-hop or two-hop depth, together with explicit temporal support. Such objects preserve local relational structure without requiring the full enterprise graph to be processed at once. They are appropriate for graph neural networks, neighborhood aggregation methods, motif-sensitive detectors, and hybrid tabular-graph encoders. In CSTS terms, they expose local relational geometry under the substrate’s typing and provenance constraints, aligning with graph-aware zero-day detection and more recent graph-contrastive intrusion detection formulations [1, 23].

4) Motif-state objects.

A motif-state object represents a recurrent local behavioral pattern expressed over canonical entities and typed relationships. Examples include fan-out authentication bursts, process-to-file write cascades, privilege-boundary traversals, repeated remote-execution chains, and short-window bipartite expansion patterns consistent with ransomware-like behavior. The purpose of the motif-state class is to elevate repeated relational structure to a first-class learning unit, allowing models to reason over local attack grammar rather than only isolated events or aggregate counts.

These object classes preserve CSTS’s entity-first semantics while making explicit the units by which downstream models consume canonical telemetry. A detector operating over CSTS need not reconstruct object boundaries from raw vendor events; instead, object construction is governed by substrate-level canonicalization, temporal semantics, and relationship typing.

Representation views.

To support modern representation learning, we further define a view of a CSTS learning object as a semantics-preserving transformation

v:o↦o~v:o\mapsto\widetilde{o}

such that o~\widetilde{o} preserves the canonical identity, typed relational interpretation, and temporal validity of the underlying object while varying its presentation to a downstream model. Views do not alter the ontology of CSTS; rather, they expose multiple valid presentations of the same underlying relational-temporal state.

Examples of valid CSTS views include:

  • •

    Attribute-masked views: selected non-critical attributes in XoX_{o} are hidden or perturbed while preserving canonical entity identity and relation typing;

  • •

    Neighborhood-subsampled views: a bounded subset of a local neighborhood is sampled while preserving the focal entity or interaction and core typed relations;

  • •

    Adjacent-window views: temporally nearby slices of the same object are formed to capture behavioral continuity or mild temporal variation;

  • •

    Partial-source views: one telemetry producer or modality is omitted while preserving canonical identity and recoverable relational meaning;

  • •

    Modality-restricted views: tabular-only, temporal-only, graph-only, or hybrid projections derived from the same underlying object.

Not every transformation is a valid view. A valid CSTS view must satisfy:

  1. 1.

    Identity preservation: canonical entity identity for focal entities must remain unchanged;

  2. 2.

    Relational validity: typed relationships must remain semantically valid under domain/codomain constraints;

  3. 3.

    Temporal consistency: the transformed object must preserve a coherent temporal support interval or a semantically admissible sub-interval;

  4. 4.

    Provenance traceability: the transformation must preserve lineage, source metadata, and confidence annotations sufficient for auditability;

  5. 5.

    Semantic admissibility: the transformation may reduce observability or alter resolution, but it must not convert the object into one with a different underlying behavioral interpretation.

These constraints are important because they connect representation learning to the portability decomposition developed later in the paper. CSTS is intended to guarantee schema stability and representational invariance at the substrate layer. Learning-object and view semantics extend that guarantee upward into model construction by specifying what bounded units may be compared, embedded, reconstructed, or contrasted across deployments. In this sense, CSTS does not merely normalize telemetry; it defines a governed representational basis for substrate-native anomaly detection, novelty detection, metric learning, contrastive learning, and graph-temporal reasoning over persistent security state [2, 15, 24, 25].

This formalism is particularly useful in the zero-day setting. A flow-centric detector may treat a focal network flow together with its surrounding host, process, credential, and neighborhood context as an interaction-state object, while a novelty or contrastive learner may compare multiple valid views of that same object across time, partial-source visibility, or deployment environment. Likewise, identity-centric detectors may operate over entity-state objects whose temporal neighborhoods are canonically comparable across enterprises. In each case, CSTS reduces dependence on brittle vendor-specific event fields and instead exposes stable learning units grounded in canonical entities, typed relationships, temporal continuity, and provenance-preserving abstraction.

Accordingly, learning objects and representation views should be understood as a Tier-4 extension of CSTS rather than a separate modeling layer. They make explicit how embedding-compatible systems consume the substrate, clarify the semantics of contrastive and metric objectives over canonical security telemetry, and prepare the ground for substrate-native zero-day detection architectures built directly on CSTS [1, 2, 15, 23, 24].

VI-E Schema Governance and Evolution

Long-term portability requires explicit schema governance. Each substrate release is versioned:

Schemav\texttt{Schema}_{v} (11)

Adapters declare compatibility with specific versions.

Backward Compatibility Rules

  1. 1.

    Additive attribute extensions are permitted.

  2. 2.

    Renaming requires alias mapping.

  3. 3.

    Removal of required fields mandates deprecation periods.

Schema evolution must preserve entity identity invariants, relationship semantics, and temporal consistency.

VI-F Representational Guarantees

CSTS enforces representational invariants at the telemetry layer:

  1. 1.

    Persistent canonical identity across ingestion boundaries,

  2. 2.

    Environment-independent relationship typing,

  3. 3.

    Explicit temporal continuity,

  4. 4.

    Governance-backed schema evolution.

These guarantees stabilize the representational boundary between telemetry ingestion and downstream modeling. CSTS does not guarantee downstream model generalization; rather, it isolates portability constraints to the representation layer, allowing modeling-level properties to be analyzed independently.

Implications

This section formalized CSTS as a time-indexed, entity-centric multigraph with explicit identity, relationship, temporal, and governance invariants. By elevating security telemetry from raw event streams to stable canonical entities and relationships, CSTS provides a structurally consistent substrate for downstream analytics. The formal definitions ensure that cross-source integration, temporal reasoning, and provenance preservation are enforced at the architectural level rather than deferred to model-specific preprocessing.

Crucially, CSTS shifts the stability requirement from machine learning pipelines to the telemetry substrate itself. Rather than compensating for drift, schema fragmentation, and identity inconsistency through retraining or adaptive heuristics, CSTS defines structural guarantees that persist across heterogeneous deployments. In doing so, it reframes cybersecurity AI fragility as a representational problem with a systematic architectural solution.

VII Case Studies

Security analytics systems frequently fail in deployment not because detection logic is weak, but because detection pipelines are tightly coupled to environment-specific telemetry schemas and brittle feature engineering layers. Even well-established techniques for lateral movement detection, anomaly detection, and ransomware identification often require substantial re-engineering across enterprises. CSTS addresses this limitation by separating detection logic from telemetry representation, providing a stable entity-relational substrate on which diverse analytical methods can operate consistently.

To illustrate the implications of this architectural separation, we reinterpret several established detection problems through the lens of CSTS. The objective is not to propose new detection algorithms, but to demonstrate that once telemetry is expressed as interactions over persistent canonical entities and typed relationships, seemingly distinct security tasks reduce to identifying structured deviations in an evolving graph. This reframing clarifies portability boundaries and reduces per-environment feature reconstruction.

VII-A Lateral Movement Under CSTS

Lateral movement detection traditionally relies on authentication sequences, credential reuse patterns, remote session behavior, and multi-host traversal analysis. Prior work demonstrates strong performance using user behavioral features engineered from authentication telemetry [4]. However, these pipelines typically reconstruct entity graphs implicitly and rely on environment-specific aggregation logic.

Within CSTS, lateral movement is interpreted as role deviation in a constrained entity-relational graph. Canonical entities such as User, Host, Credential, and Process are connected through typed relationships including AUTHENTICATES_TO, EXECUTES, and SPAWNS. Lateral movement corresponds to the emergence of traversal paths inconsistent with the historical role topology of a user or credential entity.

Signals described in [4]—such as unusual host adjacency, abnormal session patterns, or deviations from typical login rhythms—map naturally to graph deviations in CSTS: novel User→\rightarrowHost adjacencies, rapid ego-network expansion, or traversal chains exceeding typical path lengths. Rather than modeling isolated authentication events, CSTS treats lateral movement as subgraph expansion within a persistent identity graph. Because identity and relationship semantics are stabilized at the substrate layer, the detection problem becomes one of structural deviation rather than vendor-specific field engineering, improving portability across environments.

VII-B Zero-Day Threat Detection Under CSTS

Zero-day detection research frequently frames the task as anomaly detection over network telemetry augmented with structural context [1], or as a separation between anomaly detection and novelty detection via metric-learning autoencoders [2]. These approaches rely on capturing deviations from learned behavioral baselines while maintaining robustness to previously unseen attack classes.

Under CSTS, zero-day detection can be viewed as identifying relational deformation within the geometry of canonical entities and interactions. In graph-and-flow approaches [1], flows are combined with topology-aware features such as centrality and neighborhood structure. In CSTS, these structural properties arise directly from the canonical graph, where persistent identity and typed relationships define a stable interaction topology.

Operationally, anomaly detection corresponds to identifying edge or interaction patterns that cannot be reconstructed under learned substrate-consistent role geometry, aligning with autoencoder-based formulations [26]. Novelty detection can be expressed as metric separation between established behavioral manifolds and emergent relational configurations [2]. The portability benefit is that learning shifts from raw identifiers (e.g., vendor-specific fields or IP strings) to structural properties of canonical entities. Detection thus focuses on deviations in interaction structure rather than surface-level telemetry artifacts.

VII-C Ransomware as Motif Emergence

Ransomware detection is often based on file entropy signals, process bursts, or signature-like heuristics. Within CSTS, ransomware is reinterpreted as the emergence of a characteristic relational motif within the entity graph.

A canonical ransomware pattern typically includes execution of an anomalous binary, followed by rapid and high-density WRITES/MODIFIES relationships between a process entity and many file entities within short temporal windows, often accompanied by privilege boundary crossing. In graph-theoretic terms, this manifests as abrupt degree expansion and repeated bipartite interaction between a single process node and a large file neighborhood.

Cross-temporal ransomware research emphasizes detecting campaigns under changing conditions [3]. CSTS supports this objective by stabilizing identity, temporal state, and relationship semantics across deployments. Motif-based detection can therefore focus on structural replication patterns [27] rather than vendor-specific file system fields, improving cross-environment consistency.

Across these case studies, CSTS provides a unifying abstraction: lateral movement, zero-day activity, and ransomware can all be interpreted as statistically improbable relational configurations within a persistent entity graph. By stabilizing identity, relationship semantics, and temporal state at the substrate layer, CSTS reduces integration friction and clarifies the boundary between representational stability and model-level generalization. Detection logic operates over canonical interaction structure rather than brittle telemetry schemas, improving reproducibility and portability across heterogeneous enterprise environments.

VIII Deployment Model and Tiered Adoption

CSTS is designed for incremental adoption rather than wholesale infrastructure replacement. Enterprise security environments vary significantly in maturity, tooling, and integration capability. A viable representational substrate must therefore support staged deployment, allowing organizations to progressively increase semantic richness without disrupting existing pipelines.

We define a five-tier adoption model that enables enterprises to move from basic event normalization toward fully embedding-compatible, AI-native telemetry abstraction.

VIII-A Tier 0: Event Normalization

Tier 0 represents alignment with existing telemetry normalization frameworks such as OCSF [5], Elastic Common Schema (ECS) [9], and OpenTelemetry [10]. At this stage, organizations standardize field names, event categories, and log formats across vendors.

Normalization improves interoperability and reduces parsing overhead but remains event-centric. Entities are not persistently resolved, relationships are implicit, and temporal state is reconstructed downstream. Tier 0 therefore reduces syntactic inconsistency but does not address representational stability required for portable AI systems. CSTS treats Tier 0 as compatible but insufficient.

VIII-B Tier 1: Entity Resolution

Tier 1 introduces persistent canonical identity across telemetry sources. Raw observations are mapped to canonical entity types (e.g., User, Host, Process) with globally stable identifiers. This layer implements the canonical resolution function defined in the formal substrate specification, ensuring that semantically equivalent observations across heterogeneous systems map to a consistent identity.

Entity resolution is the minimal viable CSTS substrate. Once identity persistence is enforced, downstream analytics can operate over stable actor representations rather than ephemeral event records. This addresses a primary source of deployment fragility identified in ML-based security systems [21, 22], where schema variation and inconsistent identifiers degrade model portability.

VIII-C Tier 2: Relationship Materialization

Tier 2 materializes typed relationships between canonical entities, forming an explicit entity-relational graph. Authentication, process execution, file modification, network flow, and cloud interaction events are transformed into directed edges with defined domain and codomain constraints.

This tier aligns directly with graph-based detection paradigms demonstrated in prior work on lateral movement and zero-day detection [4, 1]. Instead of reconstructing relationships within each analytic pipeline, CSTS defines them once at the substrate level.

Materializing relationships reduces repeated feature engineering and enables structural pattern detection, including motif analysis consistent with established graph-theoretic foundations [27]. At Tier 2, the telemetry substrate becomes analytically expressive rather than merely normalized.

VIII-D Tier 3: Temporal Modeling

Tier 3 incorporates explicit temporal state modeling into the substrate. Entities and relationships are represented as time-indexed structures with validity intervals, rolling aggregation windows, and state transitions. This enables behavioral baselining, sessionization, and cross-entity temporal joins at the substrate layer rather than within model-specific code.

Temporal modeling is critical for anomaly detection and novelty detection systems [2]. Without explicit temporal semantics, models must infer behavioral continuity from fragmented logs. CSTS instead enforces temporal explicitness, enabling rolling behavioral state representation that remains consistent across deployments.

Temporal modeling strengthens cross-environment comparability by ensuring that behavioral state and aggregation semantics are consistent across deployments. While this does not guarantee downstream model generalization, it reduces representation-induced variability associated with evolving telemetry distributions and schema drift [21, 22].

VIII-E Tier 4: Embedding-Compatible Extensions

Tier 4 extends CSTS to support embedding-compatible representations for AI-native modeling. At this stage, canonical entities and relationships expose structured feature contracts suitable for graph embedding, contrastive learning, metric learning, and autoencoder-based anomaly detection.

Embedding-compatible extensions do not replace earlier tiers; they build upon stable identity, typed relationships, and temporal state. Prior work demonstrates the effectiveness of metric learning and representation learning for zero-day detection [2, 14, 15]. However, such models often require bespoke feature engineering tied to specific telemetry schemas.

By defining embedding interfaces at the substrate level, CSTS enables model portability across heterogeneous enterprise environments. The representational boundary ensures that learned embeddings reflect canonical relational structure rather than vendor-specific artifacts.

Tier 4 extends CSTS from structural normalization into an AI-ready substrate. By defining embedding-compatible interfaces over canonical entities and relationships, CSTS enables learning systems to operate on stable relational structure rather than vendor-specific artifacts. This preserves portability while supporting anomaly detection, novelty detection, motif reasoning, and representation learning within a unified architectural boundary.

IX Portability Decomposition Framework

CSTS is designed to stabilize telemetry representation across heterogeneous enterprise environments. However, representational stability alone does not guarantee model portability. To reason precisely about deployment behavior, we decompose portability into three distinct layers: schema stability, representational invariance, and semantic orientation stability.

This decomposition enables us to distinguish failures caused by ingestion or schema variation from failures caused by modeling assumptions under domain shift.

IX-A Schema Stability

Definition (Schema Stability).

A detection pipeline satisfies schema stability if feature definitions and aggregation logic remain unchanged under field renaming, deletion, format variation, or vendor-specific schema changes.

Schema instability manifests when upstream telemetry modifications break feature extraction, graph construction, or preprocessing pipelines. Event-centric normalization frameworks (e.g., OCSF [5]) reduce syntactic drift but do not eliminate representational fragility.

CSTS enforces schema stability by requiring that raw telemetry variations be absorbed at the adapter layer, preserving canonical entities and relationships as the stable interface to downstream models.

IX-B Representational Invariance

Definition (Representational Invariance).

A telemetry representation satisfies representational invariance if:

  1. 1.

    Entity identity persistence is maintained across ingestion boundaries,

  2. 2.

    Relationship type semantics are environment-independent,

  3. 3.

    Temporal ordering and state continuity are preserved.

Representational invariance ensures that the structural meaning of entities and relationships does not depend on vendor-specific encodings or topology-specific artifacts.

CSTS enforces representational invariance through canonical identity resolution, typed relationship constraints, temporal modeling, and governance-backed schema evolution.

Importantly, representational invariance guarantees structural comparability of entity graphs across environments but does not guarantee that learned features behave identically under domain shift.

IX-C Semantic Orientation Stability

Even when schema stability and representational invariance hold, learned features may invert or degrade under distribution shift.

Definition (Semantic Orientation Stability).

A feature ff exhibits semantic orientation stability between environments ℰA\mathcal{E}_{A} and ℰB\mathcal{E}_{B} if the sign of its class-conditional expectation remains invariant:

sign⁡(ΔA​(f))=sign⁡(ΔB​(f))\mathrm{sign}\!\big(\Delta_{A}(f)\big)=\mathrm{sign}\!\big(\Delta_{B}(f)\big) (12)

where

Δℰ​(f)=𝔼ℰ​[f∣y=1]−𝔼ℰ​[f∣y=0].\Delta_{\mathcal{E}}(f)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{E}}[f\mid y=1]-\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{E}}[f\mid y=0].

If the sign reverses, a feature that was positively correlated with malicious behavior in one environment becomes negatively correlated in another. This phenomenon represents a modeling-level portability failure rather than a representational one.

IX-D Portability Failure Modes

The decomposition above clarifies three distinct failure regimes:

  1. 1.

    Schema Failure: Feature extraction breaks due to field drift.

  2. 2.

    Representational Failure: Entity identity or relationship semantics are inconsistent across environments.

  3. 3.

    Orientation Failure: Learned feature direction reverses under domain shift despite stable representation.

CSTS is designed to eliminate the first two categories by enforcing structural invariants at the telemetry layer. However, orientation stability remains a property of the learning task and data distribution.

IX-E Implications for Detection Tasks

This framework explains why different detection paradigms exhibit different portability behavior.

Identity-centric tasks such as lateral movement detection rely heavily on stable relational topology. When canonical identity and relationship semantics are preserved, feature orientation tends to remain stable across environments.

In contrast, anomaly- and geometry-based tasks such as zero-day detection depend on global distributional properties of interaction structure. Even with representational invariance, latent geometric assumptions may shift across enterprise topologies, producing orientation instability.

This distinction motivates our experimental evaluation: CSTS should eliminate schema and representational failures, while residual degradation reflects modeling-level semantic instability rather than telemetry fragmentation.

X Experimental Validation

This section evaluates CSTS as a representational substrate for portable detection across heterogeneous enterprise environments. We empirically examine three stability properties derived from the formal definitions in Section VI: representational invariance, schema stability, and semantic orientation stability.

Specifically, we test the following hypotheses:

H1 (Representational Invariance). Enforcing canonical entity persistence and typed relational semantics improves cross-topology generalization for identity-centric detection tasks.

H2 (Schema Stability). Confining raw-schema variability to thin canonical adapter layers prevents detection collapse under field-level perturbation.

H3 (Semantic Orientation Boundary). Representational invariance does not guarantee semantic orientation stability under domain shift.

We evaluate these hypotheses on lateral movement (LM) detection derived from authentication and process telemetry [4]. To isolate representational effects, model architecture, windowing, training splits, hyperparameters, and random seeds are held constant across pipelines.

X-A Evaluation Setup

We construct two enterprise environments:

  • •

    Env A: Source training environment.

  • •

    Env B: Target deployment environment with schema variation, identifier differences, and increased benign authentication diversity.

For each environment, we compare two pipelines.

Event-Centric Baseline. Feature extraction operates directly on raw telemetry fields (e.g., user identifiers, destination hosts, timestamps, and event type labels). Features consist primarily of windowed count and cardinality statistics.

CSTS Pipeline. Raw telemetry is first mapped into canonical entities and typed relationships. Windowed features are derived from canonical identifiers, relational structure (e.g., unique destination hosts, two-hop expansion), and training-history-based rarity measures computed strictly on the training split to prevent leakage.

Both pipelines use identical 30-minute windows and identical classifier configurations. Hyperparameters, thresholds, and training seeds are held constant across experiments to ensure that performance differences reflect representational properties rather than algorithmic variation. In addition to F1 at threshold 0.5, we report AUROC and best-F1 obtained via fixed threshold sweep to decouple representation quality from calibration artifacts.

X-B Controlled Transfer Benchmark (Synthetic envA/envB)

We first evaluate CSTS under a controlled cross-topology benchmark designed to isolate representational effects from labeling sparsity, uncontrolled logging artifacts, and schema incompleteness. Unlike the external Sysmon corpora (Section X-C), this benchmark provides: (i) sufficient positive-window counts in both environments, (ii) explicit domain shift between EnvA and EnvB, (iii) reproducible transfer splits, and (iv) matched model architectures and hyperparameters across pipelines. This benchmark serves as the primary generalization evidence in this work.

X-B1 Cross-Topology Transfer: Identity-Centric Detection (Lateral Movement)

Lateral movement (LM) detection is an identity-centric deviation task: it detects abnormal interaction patterns between persistent entities (e.g., users, hosts, processes). This makes it an appropriate first test of CSTS, whose design stabilizes entity identity and typed relationships across environments. To evaluate transfer, models are trained on EnvA and evaluated both in-domain (EnvA) and cross-domain (EnvB). Transfer degradation is defined as the performance difference between in-domain and out-of-domain evaluation.

The event-centric baseline achieves strong in-domain performance (F1 =0.894=0.894), indicating that raw telemetry features can be highly predictive within a single environment. However, under cross-domain evaluation (Env A →\rightarrow Env B), performance degrades sharply (F1 =0.135=0.135; AUROC =0.660=0.660), reflecting sensitivity to environment-specific telemetry distributions.

In contrast, CSTS exhibits lower in-domain peak performance (F1 =0.378=0.378), consistent with structural inductive bias that reduces overfitting to environment-specific artifacts. Crucially, under cross-domain transfer, CSTS maintains substantially stronger performance (F1 =0.508=0.508; AUROC =0.991=0.991). Best-F1 improves from 0.1820.182 (baseline) to 0.8210.821 under transfer, indicating materially improved class separability rather than threshold tuning effects.

These results support H1: enforcing representational invariance at the entity-relational layer materially improves cross-topology generalization for identity-centric detection tasks. Because classifier architecture and training procedures were held constant, the observed performance gap is attributable to stabilized identity and interaction semantics rather than algorithmic variation. The performance gap is attributable to stabilized identity and interaction semantics rather than classifier variation, which was held constant across pipelines.

X-B2 Schema Perturbation Robustness Under Controlled Shift

To isolate representational brittleness independent of distributional shift, we introduce targeted schema perturbations (P1–P3) to EnvB. These perturbations simulate realistic vendor schema evolution and logging changes by renaming or removing fields directly consumed by the event-centric baseline. The CSTS pipeline processes identical perturbed inputs through canonical adapters with alias recovery, confining schema variability to the substrate boundary.

To evaluate robustness under telemetry instability (H3), we introduce targeted schema perturbations to the evaluation environment (Env B). Perturbations prioritize fields directly consumed by the event-centric baseline (e.g., user identifiers, destination hosts, timestamps, and event type labels), simulating realistic vendor schema evolution and logging changes.

Perturbation levels P1–P3 progressively increase renaming and deletion of baseline-critical fields. The CSTS pipeline processes identical perturbed inputs through canonical adapters with alias recovery, confining schema variability to the mapping layer.

Under targeted schema breakage, the event-centric baseline fails once critical raw columns are renamed or removed, yielding degenerate predictions. In contrast, CSTS maintains non-trivial predictive signal across all perturbation levels. While performance degrades modestly as perturbation severity increases, canonical entity resolution and typed relationship abstraction preserve sufficient structural information to sustain detection.

This result supports H2: CSTS satisfies schema stability under targeted perturbation. By isolating raw field variability within canonical adapters, detection logic remains invariant to column renaming, deletion, and format perturbation. The collapse of the event-centric pipeline demonstrates that raw feature pipelines violate schema stability under identical perturbations.

X-C External Sysmon Robustness & Smoke Tests

To complement the controlled synthetic benchmark, we run CSTS on public Sysmon-style corpora as a realism check of end-to-end operability and schema robustness under log heterogeneity. These external experiments are reported as robustness/smoke-test evidence only: labels are deterministic, ordered multi-signal proxy motifs and are sparse in the selected corpora/splits. Accordingly, we report split class counts and bootstrap confidence intervals, and we avoid making definitive external generalization claims from these results. Tables III–VI are therefore reported as robustness/smoke-test evidence only due to sparse motif-labeled positives; see Limitations for viability-gate details.

X-C1 External Pipeline Validation (splunk/attack_data)

Table III reports transfer results on splunk/attack_data. Because proxy-labeled positives are sparse (and thus threshold-fragile), we include split class counts and bootstrap CIs. These results primarily validate that the external pipeline is reproducible and that CSTS feature extraction and evaluation remain well-defined on real Sysmon-style telemetry.

X-C2 Schema perturbation robustness (splunk/attack_data)

Table IV evaluates targeted raw-schema perturbations (P0–P3) on the same external corpus. The event-centric baseline assumes strict raw column names and fails once baseline-critical fields are renamed/removed. In contrast, CSTS remains operable through alias-aware parsing and canonicalization, which confines schema variability to the adapter boundary.

X-C3 External Pipeline Validation (OTRF Security-Datasets)

Table V reports the same smoke-test evaluation on OTRF Security-Datasets. Because positive windows are again sparse, we emphasize uncertainty and class imbalance via class-count columns and bootstrap confidence intervals.

X-C4 Schema perturbation robustness (OTRF Security-Datasets)

Table VI repeats the P0–P3 robustness study on the OTRF corpus. As above, the key operational observation is that baseline parsing breaks under targeted schema changes, while CSTS remains operable via alias recovery and canonical graph construction.

X-D Limitations of External Sysmon Experiments

Our external Sysmon experiments on public corpora (including OTRF Security-Datasets and splunk/attack_data) are included to validate operational pipeline behavior and schema robustness under real telemetry, not to serve as definitive evidence of external-domain generalization. Labels in these datasets are generated using deterministic, ordered multi-signal proxy motifs (e.g., remote-execution process indicators, LM-relevant network activity, and effect evidence within a time window). While this labeling strategy reduces trivial feature–label entanglement, it produces sparse positive windows in the selected corpora/splits, and our predefined viability gates for transfer evaluation (minimum positive windows per environment and train split) were not met. Accordingly, we report bootstrap confidence intervals, split class counts, and robustness behavior under schema perturbations, and reserve stronger external generalization claims for future experiments with denser externally labeled or proxy-viable corpora.

X-E External Case Study: Producer Divergence on DARPA TC E3 (CADETS→\rightarrowTRACE)

We include a minimal external case study using DARPA Transparent Computing (TC) Engagement 3 to validate end-to-end CSTS ingestion and to probe portability limits under realistic provenance semantics. We use two TC producers as domains: CADETS (train) and TRACE (test). Rather than running a full transfer evaluation, we first apply a leakage-safe viability protocol: a multichannel novelty score is computed per time window using CSTS-derived tokens (process, file, and network channels), and a train-only quantile threshold determines which windows are labeled positive. This protocol explicitly separates (i) representational parsing/coverage from (ii) cross-domain score calibration.

Table VII summarizes the resulting producer divergence phenomenon. Token coverage is high in both producers (all channels nonempty in CADETS; ≥0.94\geq 0.94 nonempty rate for process tokens in TRACE), indicating that ingestion and canonicalization succeed. However, the entire TRACE score distribution lies below the CADETS-derived threshold: with q=0.40q=0.40, 0/160/16 TRACE windows exceed the CADETS train threshold (train threshold =3.972=3.972; TRACE max =3.879=3.879). Consequently, no test positives can be generated under train-only thresholding, and running transfer metrics would be statistically meaningless on this slice.

We therefore treat TC E3 as a portability boundary case study rather than a transfer benchmark on this slice: CSTS removes schema/field fragility and enables multichannel scoring across producers, but cross-producer score calibration can shift such that a threshold learned on one producer yields no positives on another. This is consistent with the broader portability decomposition emphasized in this work: schema stability is necessary but not sufficient, and additional mechanisms (producer-aware calibration, normalization, or semantically oriented feature construction) may be required for cross-producer deployment.

Empirically, this case study isolates a portability boundary distinct from schema perturbation: the representational substrate is stable and observable across producers, but cross-producer score orientation/calibration can shift enough to invalidate train-derived thresholding.

X-F Cross-Topology Transfer: Zero-Day Threat Detection

We next evaluate CSTS on a flow-centric zero-day threat detection (ZDT) task [1, 2]. To avoid sparsity artifacts, labels are defined at the window level with a stable positive rate (approximately 6–8% across splits). Both baseline and CSTS pipelines are trained on Env A and evaluated in-domain (Env A) and out-of-domain (Env B). All historical statistics required by CSTS features are computed strictly on the training split to prevent leakage.

Unlike the identity-centric lateral movement task, CSTS does not improve absolute cross-domain performance for ZDT under the current feature construction. Diagnostic analysis reveals a persistent polarity inversion in the CSTS cross-domain setting: AUROC computed on predicted scores falls below 0.5, while AUROC computed on inverted scores exceeds 0.5. This indicates that multiple CSTS-derived graph statistics (e.g., degree and expansion measures) reverse class direction across environments despite schema alignment and train-only stabilization transforms.

This result provides an empirical demonstration of H3. Although CSTS enforces representational invariance and schema stability, the ZDT task violates semantic orientation stability under domain shift. Several CSTS-derived graph features (e.g., degree and expansion statistics) reverse the sign of their class-conditional expectation between Env A and Env B. As a result, schema alignment is preserved while semantic alignment is not.

X-G Semantic Orientation Instability Under Domain Shift

The contrasting behavior between lateral movement (LM) and zero-day threat detection (ZDT) under cross-topology transfer reveals an important structural distinction. LM detection is primarily an identity-centric deviation task: it detects abnormal role transitions and entity interaction patterns. ZDT, in contrast, is a distributional anomaly detection problem that relies on statistical deviations in flow- and connectivity-derived features.

Under CSTS, schema alignment is preserved across environments. Canonical entities, typed relationships, and temporal aggregation windows remain stable. Feature extraction is performed over identical entity-relational abstractions in both Env A and Env B. This eliminates schema-level fragility and ensures that feature definitions do not depend on vendor-specific field names, log formats, or identifier conventions.

However, the ZDT experiments demonstrate that schema stability does not imply semantic stability. Several graph-derived features (e.g., connectivity counts, two-hop expansion measures, and degree-based statistics) exhibit cross-domain polarity inversion: the direction of their class-conditional expectation reverses between environments. In other words, features that are positively associated with anomalous behavior in the training environment become negatively associated in the target environment, despite identical canonical representation.

This phenomenon isolates a precise portability boundary. CSTS guarantees representational invariance—persistent identity, typed relational semantics, and temporally indexed state—but does not guarantee semantic orientation stability under distributional shift. The inversion observed in ZDT therefore reflects a modeling-level instability rather than a failure of canonical schema alignment. in other words, CSTS isolates semantic orientation instability as a modeling phenomenon rather than a schema artifact.

This layered interpretation clarifies that portability in cybersecurity AI decomposes into at least two separable components: (i) schema stability, which CSTS directly enforces, and (ii) semantic feature stability under domain shift, which remains an open modeling challenge. By stabilizing the representational boundary, CSTS enables more precise diagnosis of cross-environment degradation mechanisms, separating ingestion-level fragility from distributional modeling effects.

X-H Summary

Taken together, these experiments demonstrate that portability in cybersecurity AI decomposes into layered stability properties. Identity persistence and typed relational semantics (H1) materially improve cross-topology transfer for identity-centric tasks. Schema stability (H2) prevents collapse under telemetry perturbation. However, semantic orientation stability (H3) remains a distinct modeling challenge that is not resolved by canonical representation alone.

These results validate the central thesis of this work: deployment fragility is fundamentally representational, yet portability itself is multi-layered. By formalizing and empirically isolating these layers, CSTS provides a principled foundation for analyzing and improving cross-environment cybersecurity detection systems.

XI Discussion

This work argues that deployment fragility in AI-driven cybersecurity systems is fundamentally representational. Modern detection pipelines frequently entangle schema assumptions, identity resolution, relational context construction, and modeling logic within a single workflow. As a result, performance degradation under cross-topology deployment or telemetry evolution is often attributed to modeling weakness when the underlying cause is representational instability.

CSTS introduces a formally defined representational boundary that separates telemetry ingestion from detection logic. By enforcing entity persistence, typed relationship semantics, and temporal state continuity, CSTS targets representational invariance and schema stability. The experimental results clarify both the strengths and the limits of this architectural shift.

Layered Portability: Representation vs. Semantics

The empirical findings support a layered theory of portability:

  • •

    Identity-centric transfer benefits from representational invariance. In lateral movement detection, persistent canonical identities and typed relationships reduce cross-topology degradation, supporting H1: stabilizing identity and interaction semantics improves transfer across heterogeneous environments.

  • •

    Schema perturbation exposes ingestion fragility in event-centric pipelines. Renaming or removing baseline-critical raw fields causes catastrophic collapse when features are coupled directly to vendor schemas. CSTS confines such variability to thin adapters, preserving detection functionality and supporting H2.

  • •

    ZDT reveals a distinct portability boundary at the semantic layer. Although CSTS enforces representational invariance and schema stability, several graph-derived statistics exhibit polarity inversion under domain shift. This violates semantic orientation stability despite identical canonical representation across environments, supporting H3 and isolating the failure mode as modeling-level semantic variation rather than schema misalignment.

Taken together, the results indicate that portability decomposes into separable stability properties:

  • •

    Schema and representational stability (enforced by canonical entity-relational abstraction and adapter isolation), and

  • •

    Semantic orientation stability (dependent on feature construction, score calibration, and distributional alignment under domain shift).

CSTS directly addresses the first layer and isolates the second. By stabilizing representation, it converts ambiguous cross-environment failures into diagnosable semantic phenomena.

Decoupling Representation from Detection

A central architectural implication is the formal decoupling of telemetry representation from detection logic:

  • •

    Reduced coupling to raw schemas. Many deployed systems implicitly encode assumptions about field names, log formats, or vendor-specific semantics. CSTS externalizes these assumptions into adapters and a governed substrate boundary.

  • •

    Model-agnostic substrate compatibility. CSTS supports heterogeneous detection strategies—statistical anomaly detection, graph motif analysis [27], reconstruction-based methods [26], metric learning [2], and contextual graph modeling [1]—without direct dependence on raw telemetry schemas.

  • •

    Representation as an independent robustness lever. In our experiments, baseline and CSTS pipelines use identical windowing and classifier configurations; observed differences arise from representational properties rather than algorithmic changes. This isolates substrate design as a standalone architectural mechanism for improving portability.

Integration Complexity as a Systems Problem

Enterprise detection systems often incur repeated engineering effort for schema alignment, identity stitching, and relational reconstruction. While normalization frameworks such as OCSF [5], ECS [9], and OpenTelemetry [10] standardize event fields, they remain event-centric and do not formalize persistent entity identity or typed relationship semantics.

CSTS reframes integration as a systems problem with explicit substrate governance:

  • •

    From field alignment to entity-relational state. CSTS extends normalization into a governed, identity-stable, temporally indexed multigraph.

  • •

    Centralized stability contracts. Once canonical state is materialized, detection logic operates on stable structures rather than raw logs, shifting complexity from repeated analytic reconstruction to a centrally governed substrate with versioning and invariants.

  • •

    Operational impact under evolution. Perturbation results illustrate the practical benefit: schema evolution impacts adapters rather than collapsing downstream detection behavior.

Implications for AI-Native Security Architectures
