The results suggest that future AI-native security architectures should treat canonical entity-relational state as a first-class operational layer:

  • •

    Persistent substrate as shared analytic context. Rather than reconstructing relational context inside each analytic workflow, systems can maintain a durable substrate over which anomaly detection, campaign correlation, and representation learning operate.

  • •

    Semantic stability remains a modeling requirement. The ZDT findings underscore that canonical representation alone does not guarantee semantic invariance under distribution shift. Robust systems must combine representational stability with orientation analysis, calibration strategies, or domain-adaptive modeling.

  • •

    CSTS makes remaining challenges explicit. CSTS does not eliminate the need for semantic alignment methods; it provides a stable boundary that makes their necessity observable and their evaluation more principled.

In summary, CSTS reframes cybersecurity AI fragility as a layered systems problem: schema variability, identity fragmentation, and semantic instability are distinct phenomena that require distinct solutions. By formalizing and empirically isolating representational invariants, this work shows that stabilizing the telemetry substrate materially improves cross-topology robustness while clarifying the remaining modeling challenges. This layered perspective provides a principled foundation for portable, reproducible, and structurally coherent cybersecurity detection architectures.

XII Future Work

While this work formalizes the Canonical Security Telemetry Substrate (CSTS) and empirically isolates its representational impact, several research directions remain necessary to validate and extend its architectural implications.

Empirical Validation Across Heterogeneous Enterprise Environments

The most immediate priority is large-scale empirical validation across heterogeneous enterprise deployments. Prior work on graph-aware detection [1, 2] demonstrates improved robustness under topology variation, yet such systems continue to rely on environment-specific preprocessing pipelines. A rigorous evaluation of CSTS requires multi-organization deployments spanning distinct vendor stacks, authentication infrastructures, cloud platforms, and network topologies.

Future empirical studies should quantify:

  • •

    Reduction in per-deployment feature engineering effort,

  • •

    Cross-environment transfer performance under fixed model configurations,

  • •

    Stability under schema evolution and vendor updates,

  • •

    Resistance to degradation under concept drift [21, 22].

Longitudinal case studies would further evaluate CSTS behavior under real-world telemetry incompleteness, infrastructure evolution, and operational constraints. Such studies are necessary to establish the magnitude of representational stabilization in production environments.

Substrate-Native Zero-Day Detection (ZDT v3)

A natural extension of this work is the development of a next-generation zero-day detection architecture constructed natively atop CSTS rather than adapting graph and flow features post hoc. Existing zero-day detection systems [1, 2] incorporate graph context and metric learning, yet relational structure is still reconstructed within model pipelines.

A substrate-native ZDT architecture would consume canonical entities, typed relationships, and temporal state directly from CSTS, eliminating repeated relational reconstruction. Such a system could enable:

  • •

    Unified anomaly and novelty detection over canonical graph embeddings,

  • •

    Direct temporal state modeling without bespoke aggregation logic,

  • •

    Reduced dependence on environment-specific identifiers,

  • •

    Standardized cross-environment evaluation under fixed representation contracts.

This direction would provide a concrete proof-of-concept demonstrating the operational and modeling benefits of substrate-native detection systems.

Temporal Graph Transformer Architectures

CSTS models security telemetry as a time-indexed attributed multigraph, naturally supporting advanced graph neural network and temporal transformer architectures. Future research should explore temporal graph transformers operating directly over canonical entities and typed relationships, leveraging rolling state windows and edge-conditioned attention mechanisms.

Unlike sequence-based models that operate on flattened event streams, substrate-native temporal graph models can reason over structural evolution—capturing role transitions, motif emergence [27], and cross-entity propagation patterns. This may unify identity-centric detection [4], ransomware motif analysis [3], and relational anomaly detection [2] within a single modeling framework.

Such architectures would benefit directly from CSTS invariants, including stable identity resolution and constrained relationship semantics, which provide strong inductive bias for relational learning.

Agentic Detection and Response over Canonical Substrates

Beyond detection, CSTS enables the possibility of agentic security systems that reason and act over a persistent operational graph. Contemporary SOC tooling frequently reconstructs context independently across analytic modules. A substrate-centered architecture instead supports shared canonical state across detection, investigation, and response workflows.

Future research should explore agent-based systems that:

  • •

    Query and update canonical entity graphs directly,

  • •

    Perform multi-step reasoning over typed relationships,

  • •

    Simulate hypothetical attack propagation scenarios,

  • •

    Execute containment or mitigation actions with provenance-preserving updates.

Embedding-compatible CSTS representations (Tier 4) further enable integration of representation learning methods [14, 15] with symbolic reasoning layers, supporting hybrid explainable and adaptive security automation.

Collectively, these directions position CSTS not as a static schema proposal but as a foundational representational layer for AI-native cybersecurity architectures. By formalizing telemetry as identity-stable, temporally explicit relational state, CSTS enables portable detection systems, graph-native learning models, and agent-driven response frameworks that extend beyond event-centric pipelines.

XIII Conclusion

Modern cybersecurity systems increasingly rely on machine learning, graph analytics, and automated reasoning to detect lateral movement, zero-day threats, and ransomware campaigns. Yet despite substantial algorithmic progress, deployment fragility persists. Detection pipelines remain tightly coupled to vendor-specific schemas, environment-dependent identifiers, and bespoke feature reconstruction logic. Cross-topology generalization degrades, integration overhead accumulates, and representational reconstruction dominates engineering effort.

This work argues that the dominant constraint is representational rather than algorithmic. Enterprise telemetry remains fragmented and event-centric, limiting its suitability as a stable substrate for portable AI-native reasoning. Field-level normalization frameworks improve interoperability, but they do not formalize persistent entity identity, typed relational semantics, or explicit temporal state evolution—properties necessary for structurally coherent detection architectures.

To address this gap, we introduced the Canonical Security Telemetry Substrate (CSTS), an entity-first, relationship-explicit, temporally indexed representation layer that models enterprise security state as a governed multigraph with identity stability and schema evolution controls. CSTS establishes an integration boundary between heterogeneous telemetry sources and downstream analytics, elevating canonical entities and typed interactions to first-class constructs.

Empirically, we demonstrated three layered findings. First, for identity-centric detection tasks such as lateral movement, CSTS materially improves cross-topology transfer relative to event-centric baselines. Second, under targeted schema perturbation that causes raw event pipelines to collapse, CSTS preserves predictive signal by confining variability to thin canonical adapters. Third, in flow-centric zero-day detection, CSTS isolates a distinct portability boundary: while canonical schema alignment is preserved, semantic orientation stability of graph-derived features under domain shift remains a modeling-level challenge. This distinction clarifies that schema stability and semantic invariance are separable requirements for portable AI systems.

These results motivate a reframing of AI-driven cybersecurity architecture. Detection robustness is not solely a function of model complexity, but of representational stability. Canonical entity-relational abstraction reduces ingestion fragility and improves cross-environment portability for identity-centric reasoning. At the same time, durable deployment across heterogeneous environments requires semantically stable feature construction and calibration-aware modeling atop the substrate.

CSTS does not replace existing normalization standards; it extends them into a higher-order representational layer compatible with graph-native learning, embedding-based modeling, and agent-driven response systems operating over shared canonical state. By formalizing this substrate and empirically evaluating its behavior under transfer and perturbation, this work articulates both the promise and the boundary of canonical telemetry representation.

As cybersecurity systems continue to evolve toward AI-native architectures, stable, governed telemetry substrates will become foundational infrastructure. CSTS provides a principled approach to constructing that infrastructure—shifting detection from environment-specific feature engineering toward structured reasoning over persistent, identity-stable, temporally explicit relational state.

Appendix A Learning Objects, View Semantics, and Contrastive Construction over CSTS

This appendix expands the formal notion of CSTS learning objects introduced in Section VI-D. The purpose is twofold. First, it provides a more explicit construction grammar for bounded model-consumption units derived from canonical entities, typed relationships, and temporal state. Second, it clarifies how contrastive, metric, anomaly-detection, and open-set learning objectives may operate over CSTS without violating the substrate’s representational guarantees. This is especially relevant for zero-day detection architectures that combine anomaly detection, novelty separation, graph-aware context, and representation learning over canonical telemetry [1, 2, 15, 24].

A-A Object Construction as a Substrate-Level Contract

Let

Gt=(Vt,Et)G_{t}=(V_{t},E_{t})

be the CSTS graph at time tt, and let

𝒯={[ta,tb]⊆ℝ:ta≤tb}\mathcal{T}=\{[t_{a},t_{b}]\subseteq\mathbb{R}:t_{a}\leq t_{b}\}

denote admissible temporal support intervals. A learning-object construction operator is a map

Ψ:(Gt,q,τ,η)↦o,\Psi:(G_{t},q,\tau,\eta)\mapsto o,

where:

  • •

    qq is a focal query describing the target entity, interaction, or motif;

  • •

    τ∈𝒯\tau\in\mathcal{T} is the support interval;

  • •

    η\eta is a construction policy controlling hop depth, neighborhood bounds, aggregation rules, and modality exposure;

  • •

    oo is the resulting CSTS learning object.

The query qq may specify:

  • •

    a focal entity identifier, e.g., a Host or User;

  • •

    a focal typed relationship, e.g., AUTHENTICATES_TO(User, Host);

  • •

    a focal motif template, e.g., high-rate WRITES/MODIFIES expansion from one process to many files.

The construction policy η\eta may constrain:

  • •

    maximum hop depth hh;

  • •

    maximum neighborhood size kk;

  • •

    admissible entity and relationship types;

  • •

    aggregation windows and temporal rollups;

  • •

    view-exposed modalities (tabular, temporal, graph, provenance);

  • •

    provenance confidence thresholds.

This formulation is useful because it locates object construction at the substrate level rather than within individual detectors. Two downstream models can then consume different views of the same CSTS object while relying on a common representational contract.

A-B Canonical Classes of CSTS Learning Objects

A-B1 Entity-state objects

An entity-state object is centered on a single canonical entity u∈Vtu\in V_{t} over a support interval τ=[ta,tb]\tau=[t_{a},t_{b}]:

ouτ=(Vuτ,Euτ,τ,Xuτ,Puτ,ϕu),o_{u}^{\tau}=\left(V_{u}^{\tau},E_{u}^{\tau},\tau,X_{u}^{\tau},P_{u}^{\tau},\phi_{u}\right),

where ϕu\phi_{u} identifies uu as the focal entity. Typical examples include:

  • •

    host-state objects,

  • •

    user-state objects,

  • •

    credential-state objects,

  • •

    process-state objects.

Derived summaries in XuτX_{u}^{\tau} may include frequency, diversity, rarity, privilege spread, neighborhood entropy, role deviation, session cadence, and historical novelty relative to train-only baselines. Entity-state objects are appropriate when the detection task is naturally actor-centric.

A-B2 Interaction-state objects

An interaction-state object is centered on a typed relationship

r=(s​r​c,d​s​t,t​y​p​e,Ar,tr,Pr)∈Etr=(src,dst,type,A_{r},t_{r},P_{r})\in E_{t}

or on a short interaction sequence around it. The object includes:

  • •

    the focal edge rr,

  • •

    the local neighborhoods of s​r​csrc and d​s​tdst,

  • •

    temporally adjacent interactions,

  • •

    derived context from related credentials, processes, hosts, or files.

This is a natural construction for zero-day flow scoring, authentication anomaly detection, and short-window novelty assessment, particularly in settings where graph-and-flow context improves robustness across network topologies [1].

A-B3 Subgraph-state objects

A subgraph-state object is a bounded neighborhood

o𝒩τ=(V𝒩τ,E𝒩τ,τ,X𝒩τ,P𝒩τ,ϕ𝒩),o_{\mathcal{N}}^{\tau}=\left(V_{\mathcal{N}}^{\tau},E_{\mathcal{N}}^{\tau},\tau,X_{\mathcal{N}}^{\tau},P_{\mathcal{N}}^{\tau},\phi_{\mathcal{N}}\right),

where (V𝒩τ,E𝒩τ)(V_{\mathcal{N}}^{\tau},E_{\mathcal{N}}^{\tau}) is typically induced by one-hop or two-hop typed expansion from a focal entity or interaction. Subgraph-state objects support graph neural networks, neighborhood pooling, and motif-sensitive temporal reasoning. They also align with graph contrastive formulations in which relational neighborhoods, rather than isolated flat records, become the units of comparison and embedding [23].

A-B4 Motif-state objects

A motif-state object is centered on a typed local relational pattern satisfying a motif template

M=(VM,EM,κ),M=(V_{M},E_{M},\kappa),

where κ\kappa imposes additional rate, density, sequence, or temporal constraints. Examples include:

  • •

    fan-out authentication bursts,

  • •

    repeated remote-execution chains,

  • •

    process-to-many-file write cascades,

  • •

    short-window privilege-boundary traversals,

  • •

    cross-community communication bursts.

Motif-state objects are particularly useful when the threat signal is distributed across several edges and cannot be reduced to a single focal event.

A-C Feature and Modality Structure

Each object may expose one or more modalities.

Tabular modality.

This includes canonical aggregates and bounded summaries such as:

  • •

    counts and rates,

  • •

    uniqueness and diversity measures,

  • •

    rarity indicators,

  • •

    privilege spread,

  • •

    role deviation,

  • •

    local graph statistics,

  • •

    cross-window deltas.

Temporal modality.

This includes:

  • •

    short ordered event sequences,

  • •

    inter-arrival times,

  • •

    rolling summary histories,

  • •

    sessionized subsequences,

  • •

    state-transition traces.

Graph modality.

This includes:

  • •

    induced typed neighborhoods,

  • •

    edge labels and directionality,

  • •

    local motifs,

  • •

    structural signatures,

  • •

    provenance-aware edge confidence.

Provenance modality.

For auditability and deployment realism, object construction may also preserve:

  • •

    source-system identities,

  • •

    adapter lineage,

  • •

    confidence scores,

  • •

    missingness indicators,

  • •

    partial-observability masks.

This separation is useful because different downstream learners may operate on different modality subsets while remaining anchored to the same object semantics.

A-D Views and Semantics-Preserving Transformations

Contrastive and metric learning require multiple valid presentations of the same underlying object. We therefore define a view family over an object oo as a collection

𝒱⁡(o)={o~1,…,o~m}\mathcal{V}(o)=\{\widetilde{o}_{1},\ldots,\widetilde{o}_{m}\}

obtained by applying admissible transformations from a view operator family 𝔙\mathfrak{V}.

A-D1 Admissible view operators

Typical admissible operators include:

  • •

    Attribute masking ℳa​t​t​r\mathcal{M}_{attr}: hide or perturb selected non-core attributes;

  • •

    Neighborhood subsampling 𝒮n​b​r\mathcal{S}_{nbr}: sample a bounded subset of neighbors while retaining focal identity and essential relation types;

  • •

    Temporal offsetting 𝒮t​i​m​e\mathcal{S}_{time}: construct nearby support intervals around the same focal object;

  • •

    Source omission 𝒮s​r​c\mathcal{S}_{src}: suppress one telemetry source or producer while preserving canonicalized structure;

  • •

    Modality projection Πt​a​b,Πt​e​m​p,Πg​r​a​p​h\Pi_{tab},\Pi_{temp},\Pi_{graph}: expose only one modality of the same object;

  • •

    Confidence-threshold pruning 𝒫c​o​n​f\mathcal{P}_{conf}: remove low-confidence edges or attributes while preserving semantic consistency.

A-D2 View validity constraints

A transformation v∈𝔙v\in\mathfrak{V} is valid only if:

  1. 1.

    focal identity is preserved;

  2. 2.

    typed relationship semantics are not violated;

  3. 3.

    temporal support remains coherent;

  4. 4.

    provenance remains recoverable;

  5. 5.

    the transformed object retains the same underlying behavioral interpretation.

These constraints are important. Without them, contrastive learning may collapse into learning invariances that are operationally meaningless or that erase the very threat signal one seeks to preserve. The value of contrastive learning in this setting is precisely that it can encourage semantically aligned views to occupy nearby regions of embedding space while preserving separation from semantically distinct behavior [25, 15, 24].

A-E Positive, Negative, and Hard-Negative Policies

To support contrastive and metric learning over CSTS, it is useful to define pairing policies over learning objects.

A-E1 Positive pairs

A pair (oi,oj)(o_{i},o_{j}) is a positive pair when the two objects are distinct valid views of the same underlying behavioral unit or when they instantiate the same semantic role pattern under allowable deployment variation. Common examples include:

  • •

    two views of the same interaction-state object under different masking patterns;

  • •

    adjacent-window views of the same entity-state object;

  • •

    subgraph-state objects representing the same canonical actor under different source visibility;

  • •

    cross-environment objects occupying the same semantic role under stable CSTS typing.

A-E2 Negative pairs

A pair (oi,oj)(o_{i},o_{j}) is a negative pair when the two objects represent distinct behavioral units whose relational or temporal semantics should remain separable in embedding space. Examples include:

  • •

    benign host-state versus attack-associated host-state;

  • •

    unrelated interaction-state objects with different role semantics;

  • •

    dissimilar motif-state objects.

A-E3 Hard negatives

Hard negatives are especially important in enterprise telemetry. These are object pairs with superficially similar aggregate statistics but materially different relational meaning. Examples include:

  • •

    two flows with similar volume and duration but different process or credential context;

  • •

    two hosts with similar degree statistics but different role neighborhoods;

  • •

    two motifs with similar density but different typed edge composition.

CSTS is particularly well-suited for hard-negative construction because it makes entity identity, typed relations, and provenance explicit, allowing the pairing policy to use semantic context rather than only scalar similarity. This is also where metric-learning formulations remain useful: they help organize latent space geometry, especially for low-support or fine-grained attack classes [2, 14].

A-F Contrastive Objectives over CSTS Objects

Let fθ​(o)f_{\theta}(o) denote an encoder mapping a CSTS object to an embedding vector z∈ℝdz\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. Contrastive learning over CSTS objects seeks representations in which semantically aligned views are close and semantically distinct objects are separated.

A generic supervised or self-supervised contrastive objective can be expressed abstractly as

ℒc​o​n=∑iℓ⁡(zi,𝒫⁡(i),𝒩⁡(i)),\mathcal{L}_{con}=\sum_{i}\ell\left(z_{i},\mathcal{P}(i),\mathcal{N}(i)\right),

where 𝒫⁡(i)\mathcal{P}(i) and 𝒩⁡(i)\mathcal{N}(i) denote positive and negative sets constructed according to the CSTS pairing policy. The exact loss may be instantiated as supervised contrastive learning, self-supervised contrastive learning, or triplet-style metric objectives [25, 15].

In the CSTS setting, the value of such objectives is not merely generic representation quality. Rather, they encourage embeddings that:

  • •

    preserve semantic role similarity across environments,

  • •

    remain stable under partial observability,

  • •

    separate known malicious manifolds from benign manifolds,

  • •

    expose useful geometry for open-set and zero-day reasoning.

A-G Open-Set and Zero-Day Implications

The zero-day setting motivates a particularly important use of CSTS learning objects. Let o(f​l​o​w)o^{(flow)} denote an interaction-state object centered on a focal network flow. Under CSTS, this object can be expanded to include:

  • •

    source and destination host state,

  • •

    associated process and credential context,

  • •

    one-hop or two-hop typed neighborhood,

  • •

    rolling behavioral summaries over multiple windows,

  • •

    provenance-aware missingness or visibility masks.

A reconstruction-based anomaly detector may score such objects by their deviation from learned benign or expected geometry, consistent with prior autoencoder-based anomaly detection approaches [26, 1]. A metric or contrastive learner may further organize the embedding space so that known malicious behaviors form structured regions while semantically novel behavior lies at greater distance from both benign and known-malicious manifolds [2, 24]. This gives CSTS a direct role in zero-day and open-set architectures: the substrate defines the object semantics and view validity, while the downstream objective shapes the geometry.

A-H Why This Appendix Matters for CSTS

This appendix clarifies that CSTS is not only a normalization layer but also a governed representation substrate for AI-native security learning. Canonical entities, typed relationships, temporal continuity, and provenance are the substrate primitives. Learning objects are bounded constructions over those primitives. Views are semantics-preserving transformations of those objects. Pairing policies and contrastive objectives then operate over that governed space.

This layered interpretation is important for portability. Schema stability and representational invariance are enforced at the substrate layer. Contrastive and metric objectives then operate on a learning space whose semantics are already stabilized. In this sense, CSTS does not solve all downstream generalization problems by itself, but it sharply reduces the representational ambiguity under which such models are otherwise trained and deployed. It also makes explicit how CSTS can support follow-on work in zero-day detection, graph-aware novelty detection, and contrastive/open-set cyber representation learning [1, 2, 15, 23, 24].
